name: Mow Magic
summary: Connecting a service business’s brand, customer intake, CRM, and field-service workflows.
role: Operations, requirements, brand and marketing ownership; led website and custom application development.
challenge: Support both the customer experience and the records needed to estimate, schedule, perform, and document landscaping and snow-removal work.
sections: One business. Several connected needs.

My responsibilities span website creation and management, brand identity and logo, content, social media, promotions, apparel, SOPs, custom applications, CRM, and business records. The work combines operational requirements with creative and technical delivery.
Public intake with a persistent record

The Next.js source implements service content, lead validation and persistence, campaign attribution, QR routes, and optional private photo intake. Notification handling preserves a saved lead when email delivery fails. That decision separates record integrity from notification availability.
An operational view of the customer

A separate team application contains Firestore-connected client, lead, property, calendar, estimate, invoice, expense, vendor, and equipment workflows. Structured property and service records represent information needed before and after a visit.
A lightweight estimate alternative

The branded microsite is a separate implementation. Its PHP endpoint validates requests, recalculates estimates on the server, and stores lead records. Public marketing and internal operations have different data and access needs; the repositories keep those concerns separate.
Brand and process belong in the system
My work also includes the visual identity, promotional materials, apparel, process documentation, and records. Shared styling and configurable service content support consistency across touchpoints.
What the evidence demonstrates

The deliverable is a body of implemented business software plus confirmed operational and creative responsibility. It demonstrates requirements translation, customer-record modeling, workflow design, and cross-functional ownership. Revenue gains, time savings, staff adoption, and end-to-end production performance have not been measured here.
boundary: Deployment, applied migrations, production access controls, and customer/staff usage are unverified. The Next.js private portal, payments, approvals, crew dashboard, admin preview, and CSV export are documented as disabled. The team README’s PIN warning conflicts with newer authentication code; production security remains unverified. Automatic transfer between these applications is not established.

name: Everfold
summary: An invitation product with reusable themes, versioned templates, a builder, and host workflows.
tech: TypeScript · React · TanStack Start · Tailwind · Vitest
role: Product concept and experience direction. Repository inspection supports implementation details; individual code authorship is not asserted.
challenge: Make expressive invitation experiences reusable while protecting already-created invitations from later template changes.
sections: A product beyond the invitation

The repository includes builder, recipient invitation, guest, dashboard, template-studio, and theme-studio routes. These show an application implementation rather than only a visual concept. Route presence alone does not prove a finished or deployed flow.
A deliberate template boundary

The inspected applyTemplateVersion function copies a template definition into an invitation and records a template/version pin. Republishing a template therefore does not have to mutate invitations already created from it. Themes and structured blocks support reuse without hardcoding each event.
Saving is part of the experience

Inspected tests cover delayed backend confirmation, failed writes, missing rows, retries, and draft/publish ordering. These are meaningful failure scenarios for a builder: an interface should not imply that work is saved until the backend confirms it.
What is established

Source implements product routes and version-pinning logic, and the repository includes focused regression tests. Those tests were inspected, not executed as part of this portfolio build. The original README includes a build brief and Lovable provenance; its requested features are not treated as shipped outcomes.
boundary: Classified as an application in development. Live deployment, payments, delivery, RSVP completion, production persistence, accessibility, and the full customer journey have not been verified. No customer count or commercial success is claimed.

name: RunHouse Digital
summary: A service-business web experience with a configurable project estimator and transparent cost breakdown.
role: Brand and product initiative. The reviewed repository demonstrates a frontend implementation; precise personal contribution to each component is not established.
challenge: Help a prospective client understand how project scope, add-ons, and ongoing maintenance affect an indicative estimate.
sections: Scope becomes an interaction

The reviewed ProjectEstimator component lets a visitor choose a project package, toggle add-ons, and select maintenance. It derives a one-time total, monthly amount, and first-year estimate from the current selections.
Separate the pricing decisions

Package, add-on, and maintenance data are separate collections. Totals are calculated from those records rather than manually repeated across the interface. This is a concrete example of reusable data driving a customer-facing interaction.
A complete presentation structure

The repository contains home, services, work, case studies, contact, and legal page implementations. This establishes page structure, not verified client engagements or the truth of every marketing claim contained in the source.
Why feature this project

The estimator is the strongest inspected exhibit: it makes scope tangible and explains a business decision through interaction. It complements Mow Magic’s operational depth and Everfold’s product architecture.
boundary: Classified as a frontend prototype. Pricing is illustrative source configuration, not a current offer. No estimator-to-CRM integration, functioning contact submission, completed client projects, or live deployment is verified. Source marketing metrics are not reused as portfolio evidence.

name: Mow Magic Design System
summary: A data-free brand layer shared by public marketing and private operational applications.
tech: CSS tokens · Web components · Versioned releases
role: Part of Mow Magic’s brand and systems work. Repository documentation supports the reuse strategy; sole component authorship is not claimed.
challenge: Keep a consistent brand across separate applications without mixing customer data or business logic into the shared presentation layer.
sections: A useful boundary

The public package is explicitly limited to logos, color and typography tokens, and presentational components. Its documented boundary excludes credentials, customer and employee data, invoices, schedules, and application-specific business logic.
Reuse with a release contract

The README documents brand-lockup and status-badge components and requires consumers to pin an immutable semantic version. Breaking changes require a new major version. The team application documents vendoring the v1.0.0 package to avoid a production CDN dependency.
Why it matters

This is evidence of maintainability thinking: a shared identity layer can evolve independently while application-specific records and workflows stay in their own systems. It extends branding beyond a logo into a repeatable implementation pattern.
boundary: The README and team integration documentation were inspected. Production use, release integrity, visual consistency across deployments, and the rendered components were not independently tested.
